title: Carpet vs Hardwood for Resale Value in Edmonds
meta: For resale in Edmonds, hardwood wins the main floor and fresh carpet still wins bedrooms and stairs. Wills Flooring explains what buyers reward, room by room.
keywords: carpet vs hardwood resale value, does carpet hurt resale value, new carpet before selling house, hardwood or carpet in bedrooms for resale, flooring for selling a house Edmonds WA

blocks.lead: In Edmonds, hardwood on the main living level sells a house faster and photographs better, but new neutral carpet in bedrooms, on stairs and in a lower level is exactly what most buyers expect and is the smarter pre-sale spend there.
blocks.detail: Buyers punish worn, stained or dated flooring far more than they reward any particular material. The winning formula is clean hardwood where people gather and fresh carpet where they sleep, done before the listing photos.

blocks.html: Edmonds sellers are often downsizing out of a 1960s Seaview or Perrinville rambler they have owned for decades, and the flooring is the first thing the listing agent mentions. The question we get at the Lynnwood showroom is blunt: do we pay for hardwood, or is new carpet enough? The honest answer depends on the room, on what is already under the carpet, and on who is buying in Edmonds right now: a lot of retirees who want move-in ready, and a lot of younger families who want hardwood but will happily accept carpet upstairs. This post walks through both sides without a sales pitch for either floor.

blocks.text: What Edmonds buyers actually react to

items.title: Condition beats material
items.text: Agents tell us the same thing every year: a house with clean, current flooring of any kind shows better than a house with tired hardwood or matted carpet. A buyer who sees a pet stain mentally deducts far more than it costs to fix. Whatever you choose, it must look new in the photos.

items.title: Hardwood in the shared rooms
items.text: Living, dining, kitchen and entry are where buyers picture themselves. Hardwood there reads as quality and continuity, especially in the open remodels common in the Bowl and Westgate. It is also what the competing listings on the same street will have.

items.title: Carpet upstairs is not a negative
items.text: Bedrooms with fresh, neutral carpet are what most Edmonds buyers grew up with and still want for warmth, quiet and bare feet on a February morning. Nobody walks away from a house because the bedrooms are carpeted. They walk away because the carpet is beige from 1998.

items.title: Waterfront humidity shows in floors
items.text: Homes near the water and along the bluff carry more moisture year round. Buyers and inspectors look for cupped hardwood and musty carpet in lower levels. A dry, well-ventilated lower level with new carpet reassures; damp anything scares.

blocks.text: The Edmonds twist: check what is under the carpet

items.d: Lift a corner in a closet
items.text: Most 1950s to early 1970s Edmonds ramblers were built with oak strip flooring that was carpeted over in the 1980s. A closet corner tells you in two minutes whether you own a hardwood floor already.
items.note: Look for 2 1/4 in oak strips, often gray or stained but intact.

items.text: Pet stains, water marks at the sliding door and tack-strip holes along the walls all sand out. Deep black urine stains and buckled boards may need patching.
items.note: We check board thickness at a register to confirm it can be sanded.

items.text: If oak is under there, refinishing the main floor is the highest-return move a seller can make, because the material is already paid for. New carpet then goes only where there is no wood: usually a 1970s addition or the lower level.
items.note: Our published refinishing rates are on the price list linked at the end.

items.text: Bedrooms often have the same oak. Refinished wood there is a bonus, not a requirement. Sellers on a budget refinish the shared rooms and put new carpet in the bedrooms, and buyers respond well.
items.note: Continuity in the shared rooms; comfort in the private ones.

blocks.text: When new carpet is the better pre-sale spend

a.title: Choose it when
items: The room is a bedroom, stair run or lower level
There is no hardwood under the existing carpet
You are listing within a month and need a one-day install
The buyer pool is downsizers who value warmth and quiet
The rest of the house is in fair condition and you want the biggest visual lift per dollar spent

b.title: Choose it when
items: The room is the living, dining or entry level
Oak is already under the carpet and only needs refinishing
Neighboring listings in the Bowl or Seaview all show hardwood
You have four to six weeks before photos
You plan to stay a few years and sell later; wood ages better

blocks.title: Do not carpet over hardwood to save time:
blocks.text: We are asked to do this a few times a year by Edmonds sellers who want a quick refresh. Buyers' agents know to lift a corner, and hidden hardwood under new carpet reads as a seller hiding something. Refinish the wood or leave the carpet honest; never bury a floor the buyer would have paid for.
Mistakes Edmonds sellers make with flooring

items.html: Choosing a trendy carpet color. Cool gray looked current five years ago and now dates a listing. Warm greige or a soft taupe photographs neutral and matches most paint.
Buying the thinnest carpet possible. Buyers walk on it in socks at showings. A medium-density pad and a mid-grade nylon or polyester feel like quality without the cost of a premium fiber.
Replacing only the worst room. Three shades of beige carpet in three bedrooms look worse than one worn carpet did. Do all the bedrooms at once so they match.
Installing after the photos. The listing photos do the selling. Carpet is a one-day job; schedule it a week before the photographer, not the week after.

Ignoring the lower level smell. A musty daylight basement near the water needs a dehumidifier and a moisture-barrier pad, not just new carpet. Inspectors will find it. Compare notes with whether to replace carpet before selling.
Lift a closet corner in every carpeted room and note where there is hardwood.
Ask your listing agent which recent Edmonds sales you are competing with and what floors they showed.
Get one written quote that covers both: refinishing the wood you have and carpeting the rooms that need it, so you can see the whole picture.
Book flooring before paint touch-ups and photos, with a week of cushion.
Keep the receipts and the carpet warranty for the buyer's packet. New flooring with paperwork is a selling point on its own. Our carpet installation page explains what a Wills quote includes.

faq.a: Worn, stained or dated carpet does. Fresh neutral carpet in bedrooms, on stairs or in a lower level does not, and many Edmonds buyers, especially downsizers, prefer it there. Carpet in living areas, kitchens or bathrooms is what hurts a listing.

faq.q: Is it worth installing hardwood floors just to sell a house?
faq.a: On the main living level, usually yes, and especially if oak is already under the carpet and only needs refinishing. Installing brand-new hardwood throughout a house you are about to leave rarely pays back in full; buyers reward the shared rooms and accept carpet in the bedrooms.

faq.q: Should I replace carpet or offer a flooring credit when selling?
faq.a: Replace it. A credit asks buyers to imagine the finished result and manage a contractor after closing, and most discount the offer heavily. New carpet is a one-day job that changes the photos and the showings immediately.

faq.q: What carpet color is best for resale?
faq.a: A warm neutral: greige, soft taupe or a light warm gray in a medium pile with a subtle texture. It photographs cleanly, matches most wall colors and hides footprints. Avoid stark white, cool blue-grays and anything patterned.

faq.q: Do buyers in Edmonds prefer carpet or hardwood in bedrooms?
faq.a: It is split, and it leans toward carpet more than in Seattle. Retirees downsizing to Edmonds like warmth and quiet underfoot; younger families like hardwood but rarely walk away over carpeted bedrooms. Fresh carpet upstairs and hardwood downstairs satisfies both.

faq.q: Can I put new carpet over the old hardwood to sell faster?
faq.a: You can, but you should not. Agents lift a corner, and hidden hardwood makes buyers wonder what else is covered. Refinishing the wood you already own is nearly always the better return, and it is what the competing listing next door will have done.
